newsitem.title: USA: European exchanges battle over post-EMU pie.
newsitem.headline: European exchanges battle over post-EMU pie.

text.p: Leaders of Europe's financial futures exchanges went head-to-head Friday in a heated debate over which exchange will emerge victorious in the battle to win business after European currency union.

Under planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) in January 1999, member countries will merge their currencies into a single euro. The result will be fewer financial products and a race by the big futures exchanges in London, Frankfurt and Paris to secure a dwindling share of the trading pie.

"We are all conscious this is a great challenge for us because there will be less products and more competition between exchanges," Gerard Pfauwadel, chairman of Paris-based MATIF told a derivatives conference here.

Industry analysts and economists expect only one short-term interest rate contract settled in euro, although it could be traded on different exchanges. There is also expected to be only one or two benchmark bond futures, with one almost certainly based on German government debt issued in euros.

Both the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) and the Deutsche Terminboerse (DTB) trade short-term Euromark interest rate futures and long-term German debt futures, while the MATIF specializes in short-term Pibor interest rate futures and long-term notionnel futures.
Pfauwadel of MATIF, Daniel Hodson of LIFFE and Joerg Franke of Deutsche Boerse each argued that his own exchange was best placed to attract post-EMU business.
Pfauwadel said MATIF had a jump start on the other exchanges because France had already decided to quote all financial markets in euro right from the EMU start date.

"It will mean all the machinery behind the financial markets like dealer rates, settlement, repo markets...will move onto euro," he said. "I think this is an asset for us. It will give us the critical mass, and as you know in our business what's important is to be first and to have the liquidity."
To cut costs MATIF has already announced a 30 percent discount on exchange fees for all new contracts that mature after 1999.
He said the French Treasury bond market was well positioned to be one of the benchmarks of the long-term market.

Franke, general manager of Deutsche Boerse, the operating company of DTB, an electronic trading system, said he expects the number of derivatives exchanges in Europe to shrink to around 10 from 20 currently.
Electronic trading was cheaper than open outcry and will play a key role in allowing the DTB to secure business, he said.

"There will be a link, an alliance between all the exchanges, and as far as the Deutsche Boerse is concerned it's far easier to have a link on the basis of an electronic system rather than open outcry," he said.

"More and more market participants are wanting to be conncected to the DTB from London," he added. The DTB also announced at the conference that two more U.S firms have become members, bringing its U.S. contingent to six.
LIFFE, whose volumes dwarf those of DTB and MATIF, has the sheer weight to be the dominant exchange, chief executive Hodson said.
"We aim to be the dominant in two areas," he said, citing the benchmark short- and long-term products.

The position of London, one of the world's main financial centers, will help pull in business whether or not Britain goes into EMU in the first wave, while the London Clearing House, which clears all LIFFE's products, is another advantage, he said.
He added LIFFE's strategic alliances will also help expand volumes. LIFFE and the Chicago Board of Trade will begin to trade some of each other's products on May 9.
Hodson said the battle between the exchanges will result in one important change for the industry -- it will increase the use of technology in the open outcry pits.
"War...and we all stand to lose very significant amounts if we don't win this battle, does speed up technology," he said.
"In five years you will not recognize trading floors. There will be headphones, electronic trader cards, and there will be all manner of systems all over the world," he said.
